issues.legal_issue: Interference with the valuation of acquired structures in a special-leave appeal is unwarranted when the lower court applied no erroneous principle and the evidence supports its assessment.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the compensation awarded for a house and a well on the acquired land.
The Tribunal had inspected the house and found it to be in extremely dilapidated condition, with damaged foundations, walls, pillars, roof, doors and windows.
The Supreme Court found the compensation awarded for the house and well reasonable on the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to enhance the compensation for the house or the well because their valuations were reasonable and no error of principle was shown.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution concerning valuation of acquired land or property, the Court interferes only where an erroneous principle has been applied or important evidence has been overlooked or misapplied; an appellate court intervenes only when the decision is shown to be wrong. The Court relied on Atmaram Bhagwant v. Collector of Nagpur, A.I.R. 1929 P.C. 92, and Dollar Company, Madras v. Collector of Madras, [1975] Suppl. S.C.R. 403.

rule.if: special_leave_valuation_appeal and challenged_structure_compensation and (inspection_showed_severe_deterioration or evidence_supported_award) and not valuation_error_shown

predicates.special_leave_valuation_appeal: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging a valuation award in a property-acquisition case.
predicates.challenged_structure_compensation: The appellant challenged the compensation awarded for a structure or other improvement on the acquired property.
predicates.inspection_showed_severe_deterioration: The fact-finder inspected the structure and observed substantial deterioration or damage.
predicates.evidence_supported_award: The evidence before the Court supported the compensation awarded for the challenged structure or improvement.
predicates.valuation_error_shown: The appellant demonstrated that the valuation applied an erroneous principle or overlooked or misapplied important evidence.

issues.definition: When a special-leave valuation appeal challenges compensation for a structure, the compensation is not enhanced if the evidence supports the award and no valuation error is shown.

issues.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must reflect its reasonably foreseeable potential and special advantages, while allowing a reasonable deduction for development and land needed for public amenities.
material_facts: The acquired land was within municipal limits and near developed urban areas.
The land was bounded by roads, part of it had been diverted from agricultural use, and it had a house and utility connections.
Agreements concerning nearby parcels contemplated their development and sale as plots, with the purchaser paying development charges.
The evidence indicated that part of the land would need to be set aside for roads and other amenities.
The High Court considered the land’s development potential but deducted development costs and land for amenities in calculating its value.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the land’s potential value had not been adequately reflected and that the development deduction was excessive. It enhanced compensation for the land by one-sixth, setting the rate at Rs. 14,000 per acre, maintained solatium, and increased interest on the enhanced compensation to 9% until payment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 23, 24 and 25 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed by reference to what a willing vendor and willing purchaser would reasonably agree, considering the land’s legitimate uses, reasonably foreseeable potential and special advantages, but not speculative or imaginary possibilities. Potential value must be determined from available evidence. The Court relied on Gajapatiraju v. Rev. Divisional Officer, A.I.R. 1939 P.C. 98; Mahabir Prasad Santuka v. Collector, Cuttack, [1987] 1 S.C.C. 587; and U.P. Government v. H.S. Gupta, A.I.R. 1957 S.C. 202.

rule.if: acquired_land_compensation_case and land_near_developed_urban_area and (land_had_development_indicators or comparable_plot_transactions_supported_development_potential) and development_potential_underreflected and development_deduction_exceeded_reasonable_allowance

predicates.acquired_land_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.land_near_developed_urban_area: The acquired land was within or near a developed urban area.
predicates.land_had_development_indicators: The land had features such as road access, partial diversion, buildings or utility connections that supported its suitability for development.
predicates.comparable_plot_transactions_supported_d: Transactions involving comparable parcels supported the prospect of developing and selling land in plots.
predicates.development_potential_underreflected: The lower valuation did not adequately account for the land’s reasonably foreseeable development potential and special advantages.
predicates.development_deduction_exceeded_reasonabl: The lower valuation deducted more for development costs or land needed for amenities than the evidence reasonably supported.

issues.definition: Where acquired land near urban development has evidence-based development potential that was underreflected and subjected to an excessive development deduction, its compensation is enhanced to reflect reasonable potential value.
